report.releaseDate: Oct 2026 (CT DCP Open Data monthly update for September 2026; operator payments due 15 Oct; trade coverage 20–23 Oct 2026)
report.verdict: Connecticut's September 2026 data show a closed, three-licensee market that is still growing but visibly decelerating: record online-casino wagers of $1.95bn (+6% YoY) produced ~$57m of taxable GGR (+6% YoY, versus +17% in August), while sports handle rose 7% to $246.3m on an 8.9% hold and DraftKings overtook FanDuel in sports revenue. September was also the last month at the 18% iGaming tax — the statutory step-up to 20% took effect in October 2026 — so the state's take rises just as organic growth slows. For an outside operator the B2C door is shut by statute; the only realistic routes are B2B supply or displacing an incumbent partner at contract renewal.
summary: **A duopoly-plus-lottery market by statute.** Public Act 21-23 (2021) and the amended tribal-state compacts confine Connecticut to three master wagering licensees — the Mashantucket Pequot Tribal Nation (MPI Master Wagering License CT, LLC → DraftKings), the Mohegan Tribe (Mohegan Digital, LLC → FanDuel) and the Connecticut Lottery Corporation (CLC → Fanatics Sportsbook). Two online casinos, three online sportsbooks, no commercial land-based casinos. Regulator: Department of Consumer Protection (DCP) Gaming Division.

**Record iGaming wagers, but growth has halved.** September 2026 online-casino wagers hit an all-time high of $1.95bn (+6% YoY). Gross win was $67.0m (+6.5% YoY vs $62.9m) and taxable GGR after promotional deductions ~$57m (+6% YoY vs $53.7m in Sep-25). August had grown +17% YoY ($58m taxable), so the annual growth rate fell by roughly two-thirds in a single month.

**Hold and promo arithmetic are stable.** Gross win of $67.0m on $1.95bn of wagers is a ~3.4% hold; the ~$10m gap between gross win and taxable GGR (~15% of win) indicates both operators are using the full 15% statutory promotional-deduction cap. Implied state payment at 18% ≈ $10.3m for the month [estimate].

**Connecticut is the #4 US iGaming state and still punches above its weight per capita.** The $67.0m gross win was 6.6% of the seven-state US total of $1.02bn in September (PA $316.8m, MI $300.2m, NJ $274.8m, CT $67.0m, WV $39.5m, DE $15.0m, RI $5.9m). CT's 6.5% growth was the slowest of the seven states (US +12.9%). CY2025 iGaming gross win of $707.5m on ~3.6m residents is ~$195 per head [estimate].

**FanDuel/Mohegan leads iGaming and is pulling away.** Per Chris Altruda's analysis of DCP data, FanDuel's year-to-date (Jan–Aug 2026) gross-win growth was +23.2% versus DraftKings' +6.9%, extending FanDuel's lead to $27.5m YTD from $3.8m for all of 2025; FanDuel topped $30m/month for 11 straight months while DraftKings fell below $30m in each of the three months to August.

**Sports betting: $246.3m handle (+7% YoY), $21.4m GGR, $2.47m tax.** Online handle was $238.3m (Covers) — i.e. 96.7% of total — leaving retail at ~$8.0m [derived]. Hold recovered to 8.9% from 7.1% in September 2025. Tax of $2.47m at 13.75% implies taxable GGR of ~$18.0m [derived], so sportsbooks deducted ~$3.4m of promotional credits/excise.

**DraftKings overtook FanDuel in sports revenue.** DraftKings (MPI) reported $7.32m versus FanDuel (Mohegan Digital) $7.0m (-6% YoY), reversing a $1.64m FanDuel lead in Sep-25. Online handle shares: DraftKings 41.6% (~$99.1m, up from 40.2%), FanDuel 37.2% ($88.7m, +1.7% YoY, down from 39.4%), CLC/Fanatics 21.2% ($50.5m, +11.3% YoY despite cutting promos 73%).

**The CY2025 base is ~$1bn of online revenue.** AGA State of the States 2026: total commercial (online) gaming revenue $973.4m (+27.9%) — iGaming $707.5m (+31.7%), sports $265.9m (+18.8%) — generating $139.1m of state tax. DCP's own 2025 at-a-glance figures: $108.27m online-casino payments and $29.44m online sports-wagering payments to the state, consistent with ~$601m of taxable iGaming GGR and ~$214m of taxable online sports GGR [derived].

**Land-based is a 25%-of-slot-win franchise.** Under the 1993/1994 MOUs each tribe pays 25% of gross slot win in exchange for casino exclusivity. CY2025 slot contributions were $218.87m (DCP), implying ~$875m of combined slot win [derived]. Foxwoods reported $30.2m September 2026 slot win and a $7.6m payment (Aug-26: $34.1m / $8.53m, the 2026 peak); Mohegan Sun's September figure was not retrieved [n/a]. Table-game revenue is not shared with the state and not disclosed.

**Total 2025 gaming transfers to the General Fund: $692.7m (DCP).** Of this, online casino $108.3m, online sports $29.4m and slots $218.9m; the balance is predominantly CT Lottery transfers [composition unverified].

**Tax regime: GGR-based, with a scheduled step-up.** CGS §12-866(b): online casino GGR taxed at 18% for five years from first licence (Oct 2021), 20% for all periods after September 2026 — confirmed in the DCP dataset note. Sports wagering (online and retail) and fantasy contests: 13.75% of GGR. Promotional deductions for iGaming capped at 25% of win (Oct-21–Sep-22), 20% (Oct-22–Sep-23), 15% thereafter. The 0.25% federal excise on sports handle applies on top.

**The October 2026 step-up is worth ~$14m/yr to the state [estimate]** — two points on ~$57–60m of monthly taxable GGR is ~$1.1–1.2m/month — and it lands as organic growth slows, so operator margins compress on both fronts. No change to the 13.75% sports rate is scheduled.

**Licensing is tiered and the top tier is full.** Master wagering licences (tribes, CLC) sit above online gaming operator licences (DraftKings, FanDuel, Fanatics), online gaming service provider licences (platform, content, payments, geolocation, KYC vendors), sports wagering retailer licences (CLC's up-to-15 retail books, incl. the XL Center since Sept 2023) and occupational licences. Online gaming operator licence fee: $250,000 initial [renewal amount unverified]; tribal master licences carry 10-year initial terms [renewal terms unverified].

**Enforcement has hardened in 2025–26.** Connecticut enacted the first US sweepstakes-casino ban (SB 1235, effective 1 Oct 2025), DCP issued cease-and-desist orders to unlicensed online operators in 2025, is litigating against Kalshi, and in September 2026 Governor Lamont announced new actions with DCP ordering nine prediction markets to stop offering sports-event contracts to Connecticut residents.

**Responsible gambling and advertising rules are mainstream-US-strict.** 21+ for online casino and sports (18+ lottery), in-state geolocation, DCP self-exclusion, mandatory deposit/time-limit tools, no marketing to under-21s or on college campuses, and no wagering on in-state college teams (outside tournaments) or individual college-athlete props [per PA 21-23; specific clauses not re-read this session].

**Payments are mainstream US rails.** Operators offer ACH/online banking, debit cards, PayPal/Venmo, Play+ prepaid and cash at the tribal cages; whether credit-card funding is permitted under the DCP regulations was not verified this session [unverified].

**Political direction: fiscal, protectionist, enforcement-led.** The legislature's revealed preference is to protect the tribal/CLC revenue stream (the 25% slot share is conditional on exclusivity), raise take at the margin (20% iGaming) and push out unlicensed substitutes. A Vermont-style revenue-share comparison (VT keeps 2.7c per $ bet vs CT 1c) is already being used by commentators to argue CT's sports rate is low — a 2027-session tax debate is plausible.

**Read-through for B2Tech: B2C entry is statutorily closed; the play is B2B or partner displacement.** Each tribe may appoint one online gaming operator and CLC one; those slots are held by DraftKings, FanDuel and Fanatics (Fanatics replaced Rush Street/PlaySugarHouse at CLC in 2023, proving displacement is possible). The accessible route is an online gaming service provider licence (platform/content/payments) — a ~$67m/month iGaming market with only two aggregators is attractive for content supply — or positioning for the next tribal/CLC partner renewal. Economics to model: 20% GGR tax, 15% promo cap, tribal revenue share, and a decelerating ~6% growth market.

segments.name: Online casino (iGaming)
segments.headline: Record $1.95bn wagers and $67.0m gross win in September, but YoY growth collapsed from +17% to +6% in the final month at the 18% rate.
narrative: Connecticut's two online casinos — DraftKings (under the Mashantucket Pequot's MPI Master Wagering License CT, LLC, branded with Foxwoods) and FanDuel (under Mohegan Digital, LLC, marketed as Mohegan Sun Casino) — took a record $1.95bn of wagers in September 2026, up 6% year on year, according to Gaming Intelligence's reading of the DCP release. Gross win (the DCP 'Online Casino Gaming Win/(Loss)' line, before any deductions) was $67.0m against $62.9m in September 2025, a 6.5% rise, equivalent to a ~3.4% hold on wagers — a ratio that has barely moved since launch and is typical of a slots-heavy, high-velocity iGaming mix. The twelve months to September 2026 produced roughly $665m of taxable GGR and close to $120m of state payments on the secondary tallies we saw, versus a DCP-reported $108.3m for calendar 2025.

The number that matters for tax is taxable GGR: gross win less the statutory promotional deduction, which since October 2023 has been capped at the lesser of 15% of win or actual promotional coupons/credits wagered (DCP dataset note 4, Public Act 21-23). Poker Industry PRO puts September taxable GGR at ~$57m, +6% on the $53.7m of September 2025, which implies ~$10m of promotional deductions — essentially the full 15% cap — and a state payment of roughly $10.3m at 18% [estimate]. That is a materially weaker print than August ($58m taxable, +17% YoY) or March 2026's all-time high of $59.7m; one month is not a trend, but the deceleration is sharp enough that the October tax step-up will be absorbed in a slower market than legislators assumed when the five-year schedule was written in 2021.

Competitive dynamics inside the duopoly have shifted decisively toward FanDuel. On Chris Altruda's analysis of the DCP operator lines, FanDuel/Mohegan grew gross win 23.2% year-to-date through August 2026 against 6.9% for DraftKings/Foxwoods, widening its lead to $27.5m for the first eight months of 2026 from just $3.8m across all of 2025; FanDuel cleared $30m of monthly gross win for eleven consecutive months and topped $35m in July, while DraftKings slipped below $30m in June, July and August. That implies a FanDuel share in the mid-50s per cent and DraftKings in the mid-40s [estimate; exact operator split for September not retrieved]. In a two-operator market with a 15% promo cap, share gains come from product (live dealer, exclusives such as DraftKings' in-house titles) and cross-sell from sportsbook rather than bonus intensity, which is capped in its tax efficiency — a point of direct relevance to any content or platform supplier assessing the B2B opportunity.

Nationally, Connecticut remains the fourth-largest of seven US iGaming states, contributing $67.0m (6.6%) of the $1.02bn September total, but it was the slowest-growing of the seven (US +12.9%; Michigan +15.9%, New Jersey +13.0%, Pennsylvania +10.5%). The CY2025 gross win of $707.5m (+31.7%, AGA) equates to roughly $195 per resident [estimate], among the highest penetration rates in the country, which argues that the market is approaching maturity and that future growth will track population spending power rather than channel conversion.

Commercially, the segment is closed to new B2C entrants: each tribe may contract with a single online gaming operator and CLC is not authorised for online casino. The only addressable entry points are (i) an online gaming service provider licence to supply content, platform, payments or compliance tooling to the two licensed operators, and (ii) positioning for a tribal partner change when the DraftKings–Foxwoods or FanDuel–Mohegan agreements come up for renewal [contract terms not public]. Any supplier model should assume a 20% GGR tax from October 2026, a 15% promo cap, and tribal revenue-share economics on top of operator margin.

segments.name: Sports betting (online & retail)
segments.headline: $246.3m handle (+7%), 8.9% hold, $2.47m tax; DraftKings takes the revenue lead as FanDuel stalls and Fanatics/CLC grows 11% on 73% less promo.
narrative: Connecticut bettors staked $246.3m in September 2026, up 7% year on year on LegalSportsBetting.com's reading of the DCP data (our own comparison against rg.org's $221.6m September 2025 total gives closer to +11%; the gap appears definitional — whether CLC retail is inside the Sept-25 base — and is unresolved). Online handle was $238.3m per Covers, so retail across the two tribal sportsbooks and CLC's venues was only ~$8.0m, 3.3% of the total, versus $8.72m a year earlier: retail is structurally shrinking in absolute terms even as the market grows. Gross revenue of $21.4m equates to an 8.9% hold on online handle (8.7% on total), a recovery from the 7.1% of September 2025 and the 8.3% of May 2026, and still below the 11.3% averaged over calendar 2025 when operator-friendly results inflated the base.

Tax receipts of $2.47m at the flat 13.75% rate imply taxable GGR of ~$18.0m [derived], meaning operators deducted roughly $3.4m of promotional credits and federal excise from the $21.4m gross figure. The state's effective take was about 1 cent per dollar wagered — a figure now being contrasted unfavourably with Vermont's 31.7% revenue share (2.7c per dollar) in trade commentary, and the kind of comparison that tends to precede a tax bill.

Operator positions moved. DraftKings (MPI) booked $7.32m of revenue against FanDuel's (Mohegan Digital) $7.0m, flipping September 2025 when FanDuel led by $1.64m; FanDuel's handle grew just 1.7% to $88.7m while its revenue fell 6%. DraftKings' online handle share rose to 41.6% (~$99.1m [derived]) from 40.2%; FanDuel slipped to 37.2% from 39.4%; the CLC/Fanatics book grew online handle 11.3% to $50.5m (21.2%) despite cutting promotional spend by 73% — the clearest evidence in the data that Fanatics has moved from acquisition to margin mode in its third year as CLC's partner. The operator revenue figures appear to be on the DCP post-deduction basis [basis unverified], since the three operators plus retail reconcile to the ~$18.0m taxable total but not to the $21.4m gross total.

The calendar-2025 base against which this is measured: handle of $2.34–2.37bn (Covers / rg.org), gross revenue $263–266m (Covers / AGA, +18.8%), taxable revenue ~$198.5m (rg.org) and DCP-reported online sports payments of $29.44m. Year-to-date 2026 (Jan–Sep) online handle is $1.74bn with $161.3m gross revenue and a 9.2% hold (Covers), tracking modestly ahead of 2025 on handle but behind on revenue because of the hold normalisation. Lifetime since October 2021, LegalSportsReport counts $9.19bn of handle, $973m of revenue and $105.8m of taxes.

Structurally the sports vertical is a three-licence market: the two tribes (one skin each, online and retail at Foxwoods and Mohegan Sun) and CLC (one online skin, up to 15 retail locations under statute, including the XL Center in Hartford since September 2023). Prohibited markets include in-state college teams outside tournaments and individual college-athlete proposition bets [per PA 21-23; not re-read this session]. The enforcement perimeter widened in September 2026 when DCP ordered nine prediction-market platforms to stop offering sports-event contracts to Connecticut residents, alongside the state's pending lawsuit against Kalshi — a direct defence of the licensed books' handle. For an outside operator the realistic angle is again B2B (pricing, risk, platform) or the CLC skin at its next partner review; CLC has already changed partners once (Rush Street → Fanatics, 2023).

segments.name: Land-based tribal casinos & lottery (retail)
segments.headline: The 25%-of-slot-win franchise delivered $218.9m in 2025; Foxwoods' $30.2m September slot win was down from the August peak, and retail sportsbooks are a rounding error.
narrative: Connecticut has no commercial casinos. Foxwoods (Mashantucket Pequot Tribal Nation) and Mohegan Sun (Mohegan Tribe) operate Class III gaming under 1991/1994 compacts and 1993/1994 memoranda of understanding under which each tribe remits 25% of gross video-facsimile/slot win to the state's General Fund for as long as no other party is permitted to operate slots or commercial casino games in Connecticut (DCP Gaming Division FAQ). Table-game revenue is not shared and not published. The exclusivity condition is the single most important structural fact in Connecticut gaming policy: any commercial casino, VLT or third-party iGaming expansion would put ~$219m a year of slot contributions at legal risk, which is why the 2021 expansion was built through the tribes rather than around them, and why the planned joint tribal casino at East Windsor (Tribal Winds) has been shelved to 2032.

DCP reports total slot contributions of $218.87m for calendar 2025, implying ~$875m of combined slot win [derived]. Monthly 2026 data (DCP, via Foxwoods releases and the UNLV Center for Gaming Research compilation) show Foxwoods slot win of $30.6m in March, $29.6m in April, $32.9m in May and July, a 2026 high of $34.1m in August ($8.53m payment) and $30.2m in September ($7.6m payment, with >$19m paid out in 2,600+ jackpots). Mohegan Sun is the larger property — first-quarter 2026 win of $126.4m (+5.65%) on $1.51bn handle across 3,393 machines versus Foxwoods' $86.4m (-0.75%) on $1.01bn across 3,252 machines — but its September 2026 figure was not retrieved [n/a]. Cumulatively the Mashantucket Pequot have paid more than $4.9bn to the state since 1993.

Retail sports betting is marginal and shrinking: ~$8.0m of September handle across the two casino sportsbooks and CLC's retail venues, versus $8.72m a year earlier; in June 2026 the statewide retail channel produced $6.9m handle, $0.72m GGR and $97k of tax (DCP retail dataset via theplaybookusa). CLC's statutory allowance of up to 15 retail locations (XL Center from September 2023) has not changed the picture — Connecticut is a >96%-online sports market and the retail books function as brand anchors for the online skins rather than profit centres.

The Connecticut Lottery Corporation is the third master licensee and the largest single contributor to the $692.7m of 2025 gaming transfers to the General Fund [lottery component unverified; FY2026 sales and transfers not retrieved — n/a]. Its strategic relevance to an outside operator is twofold: it is the only non-tribal route to an online sports skin (currently Fanatics), and it is the entity most likely to seek expanded online authority (iLottery/online draw games) in future sessions — a development that would alter the online channel mix without disturbing tribal exclusivity on casino games.

Host-community pressure is building: officials in the casino towns lobbied in 2026 for a larger direct share of slot revenue. Any reallocation would be fiscal rather than commercial, but it is a reminder that the 25% slot share is a political settlement as much as a contract, and that the state's appetite for gaming revenue remains undiminished.

segments.name: Licensing & tax regime
segments.headline: Three master licences, one skin each, GGR-based taxes — and the five-year iGaming introductory rate expired with the September 2026 period.
narrative: The framework is Public Act 21-23 (HB 6451, signed 27 May 2021), codified at Chapter 229a of the Connecticut General Statutes (§§12-850 et seq.), together with the July 2021 amendments to the Mashantucket Pequot and Mohegan compacts and MOUs (approved by the US Department of the Interior and published in autumn 2021) and DCP's implementing regulations (Regs. Conn. State Agencies, online gaming regulation file no. 6354). Online casino gaming and sports wagering launched on 12 October 2021 (soft launch; the DCP dataset dates online casino operations from that day). DCP's Gaming Division licenses, audits and publishes monthly data; the Attorney General and DCP share enforcement.

Licence architecture is tiered. Master wagering licences are available only to the two tribes (online casino, online and retail sports wagering, fantasy contests, keno) and to CLC (online sports wagering, up to 15 retail sports wagering locations, fantasy, and online lottery draw games). Each master licensee may contract with one online gaming operator — hence DraftKings (Foxwoods), FanDuel (Mohegan Sun) and Fanatics (CLC, which replaced Rush Street Interactive's PlaySugarHouse in 2023). Beneath these sit online gaming service provider licences (platform, content, payment processing, geolocation, identity vendors), sports wagering retailer licences, and occupational licences for key employees. Tribal master licences carry ten-year initial terms [renewal mechanics unverified]; the online gaming operator licence carries a $250,000 initial fee [renewal fee unverified]; retailer and service-provider fees were not verified this session [unverified].

Tax is levied on gross gaming revenue, defined as wagers less winnings paid, less a capped promotional deduction, and (for sports) less the 0.25% federal excise. Online casino GGR is taxed at 18% for the five years from the first licence and 20% thereafter — CGS §12-866(b), confirmed by DCP dataset note (5): '18% of Gross Gaming Revenue until September 2026; 20% for all subsequent periods'. Sports wagering, online and retail, and fantasy contests are taxed at 13.75% of GGR. The promotional deduction for online casino was limited to 25% of win in year one, 20% in year two and 15% from October 2023 (note 4); operators have consistently used the full cap, so effective tax on gross win has been ~15.3% and will be ~17.0% from October 2026 [derived]. A June 2025 DCP note records MPI (DraftKings) amending its March and April 2025 returns to reduce reported promotional coupons by $4.97m and $5.12m after a back-end categorisation error — evidence that DCP audits the promo line closely.

The state's gaming tax take is therefore layered: 2025 online casino payments $108.3m, online sports $29.4m, retail sports ~$1.4m [derived], and 25% slot contributions $218.9m — about $358m before lottery transfers, within DCP's $692.7m total General Fund transfer. The AGA's $139.1m 'gaming tax revenue 2025' corresponds to the online verticals only. On ~$57–60m of monthly taxable iGaming GGR, the two-point step-up adds roughly $1.1–1.2m per month, or ~$14m a year [estimate], without legislative action.

Commercially, the regime is explicit about who can hold the economics: the tribes and CLC own the licences, the operators are contracted vendors, and all other participants are service providers. There is no competitive tender, no auction, and no mechanism for additional online skins without reopening the compacts — which would in turn jeopardise the 25% slot share. For B2Tech this means the Connecticut licence to pursue is the online gaming service provider licence; the fee and processing timetable should be confirmed directly with DCP [unverified], and any content or platform agreement will sit two contractual layers below the master licence.

segments.name: Payments, responsible gambling, advertising & enforcement
segments.headline: Mainstream US payment rails, 21+ with geolocation and self-exclusion, and an enforcement posture that has moved from sweepstakes (2025) to prediction markets (2026).
narrative: Payments follow the US regulated template: ACH/online banking (via aggregators such as Trustly/Plaid), debit cards, PayPal and Venmo (FanDuel), Play+ prepaid cards and cash at the Foxwoods and Mohegan Sun cages; FanDuel markets sub-one-hour PayPal withdrawals as a differentiator. Whether credit-card funding is permitted under DCP's online gaming regulations was not verified in this session [unverified]; an operator or payments supplier should confirm against the regulation text before modelling deposit mix. There is no mobile-money or cash-voucher dimension to speak of — the payments opportunity for a B2B supplier is in instant-withdrawal, fraud and identity tooling rather than in rails.

Responsible-gambling requirements are set in statute and regulation: players must be 21 or older for online casino and sports (18 for lottery), physically located in Connecticut (geolocation enforced), and operators must offer deposit, spend and time limits, cooling-off periods and participation in DCP's voluntary self-exclusion programme covering online and retail; master licensees fund problem-gambling treatment through statutory contributions to the chronic gamblers treatment and rehabilitation account [amounts unverified this session]. Advertising rules prohibit marketing to under-21s and on college campuses and require responsible-gambling messaging; wagering on in-state college teams (outside multi-team tournaments) and on individual college-athlete props is prohibited [per PA 21-23; specific clauses not re-read].

Enforcement is where the regulatory direction of travel is clearest. In 2025 Connecticut became the first state to enact a sweepstakes-casino prohibition (SB 1235, effective 1 October 2025), which also outlaws unlicensed online casino and sports offerings and lottery courier services; DCP issued cease-and-desist orders to unlicensed online operators during 2025. In 2026 the focus turned to prediction markets: the state is litigating against Kalshi, and in September 2026 Governor Lamont announced new actions under which DCP ordered nine prediction-market platforms to stop offering sports-event contracts to Connecticut residents. Each move protects the licensed books' handle and the state's 13.75%/20% take — the political economy is squarely aligned with incumbents.

For an operator or supplier the compliance bar is therefore conventional-US-strict but predictable: DCP audits monthly returns line by line (see the 2025 MPI promo restatement), publishes operator-level data within ~two weeks of month-end, and has shown willingness to use C&D orders and litigation against grey-market substitutes. The corollary is that any product adjacent to the perimeter — sweepstakes, social casino with cash-out, event contracts, skill-game cabinets — should be assumed hostile territory in Connecticut.

highlights.text: Scale and density: a ~$67m/month gross-win iGaming market and ~$21m/month sports GGR on 3.6m people — roughly $195 iGaming gross win per resident in 2025 [estimate], one of the highest penetrations in the US — served by just two casino aggregators. Content, live-dealer and platform suppliers face an unusually concentrated and reachable buyer set.

Partner displacement is proven possible: CLC replaced Rush Street with Fanatics in 2023, and Fanatics has since grown online handle 11.3% YoY while cutting promos 73%. The next CLC or tribal partner review is the only B2C route in, and the CLC skin (21.2% handle share) is the most contestable.

Transparent, operator-level monthly data (wagers, win, promo, payments by licensee on CT Open Data) and a predictable, GGR-based tax code with the only scheduled change (18%→20%) now behind the market — low regulatory-surprise risk for business planning.

Enforcement protects the licensed perimeter: the 2025 sweepstakes ban and the September 2026 prediction-market cease-and-desist orders remove substitutes and channel demand to licensed products — a tailwind for anyone inside the tent.

FanDuel's iGaming momentum (+23.2% YTD vs DraftKings +6.9%) shows product-led share shift is achievable even under a 15% promo cap; DraftKings' sports revenue lead in September shows the sports race remains open — both argue that supplier differentiation (exclusive content, risk/pricing) is monetisable here.
Sports hold recovered to 8.9% from 7.1% a year earlier, lifting GGR despite only +7% handle; YTD online hold of 9.2% is a healthier base than the 11.3% outlier of 2025 for underwriting 2027 revenue.

lowlights.text: B2C entry is closed by statute and compact: one online operator per tribe, one for CLC, no tender mechanism, and any expansion would jeopardise the 25% slot share (~$219m/yr) that underpins tribal exclusivity. Realistic access is B2B only.

Growth is decelerating fast: iGaming taxable GGR growth fell from +17% (Aug-26) to +6% (Sep-26) and Connecticut was the slowest-growing of the seven US iGaming states in September (US +12.9%). Per-capita penetration suggests approaching maturity.

Tax step-up to 20% of iGaming GGR from October 2026 lands on a slowing market; combined with the 15% promo cap, effective tax on gross win rises to ~17% [derived], compressing operator (and therefore supplier revenue-share) economics by ~2 points.

Sports economics are thin and politically exposed: the state kept ~1c per dollar wagered in September versus Vermont's 2.7c, and commentators are already framing the 13.75% rate as low — a 2027-session rate debate is plausible.
Retail is structurally irrelevant (~3% of sports handle and shrinking in absolute terms), so any land-based or omnichannel proposition has no addressable market outside the two tribal resorts.

Perimeter products are hostile territory: sweepstakes, event contracts and unlicensed online offerings have been met with legislation, C&D orders and litigation (Kalshi) within 12 months — regulatory risk for anything not squarely inside the three-licence framework.

Data gaps this session: Mohegan Sun September slot win, Fanatics' sports revenue, the September iGaming operator split, licence-fee renewal schedules and CT Lottery FY2026 figures could not be verified [n/a]; the +7% vs ~+11% sports-handle YoY discrepancy is unresolved.

forecast.intro: The single scheduled regulatory change has now happened: September 2026 was the final month at the 18% introductory iGaming rate written into Public Act 21-23, and from the October 2026 period the state takes 20% of online-casino GGR (CGS §12-866(b); DCP dataset note). On the current ~$57–60m of monthly taxable GGR that is worth ~$1.1–1.2m a month, or ~$14m a year, to the General Fund [estimate] — pushing annual iGaming payments from ~$120m (12 months to Sep-26) toward ~$135–140m at flat volumes. The sports rate (13.75%) and the 15% promo cap are unchanged; the licence count (3/2/3) is fixed by statute. The moving parts for 2027 are therefore political rather than scheduled: a possible sports-rate debate, further prediction-market and sweepstakes enforcement, CLC's push for broader online authority, and host-town demands on the slot share.

forecast.view: **Market:** we expect Connecticut online-casino gross win to grow mid-to-high single digits over the next 12 months (CY2026 gross win ~$770–790m, CY2027 ~$820–860m [estimates]), with taxable GGR tracking ~85% of that given full use of the promo cap; the September deceleration to +6% is partly a tough comparison against a record September 2025 but the per-capita data argue the channel-conversion phase is over. Sports handle should grow mid-single digits with hold mean-reverting toward 9–10%, implying CY2026 GGR of ~$215–230m [estimate], below 2025's hold-inflated $263–266m. **Margins:** the 20% rate takes ~2 points out of operator iGaming margin from October; FanDuel's share gains suggest it, not DraftKings, is best placed to absorb this, and we expect the iGaming share gap to widen further before any DraftKings response. **Rules:** base case is no legislative change in 2027 beyond enforcement bills; the tail risk is a sports-rate increase (Vermont/NY comparisons are already in circulation) or a promo-cap tightening. Tribal exclusivity makes an additional skin or commercial casino effectively a zero-probability event before 2032. **Leverage/structure:** the state's dependence on gaming (~$693m of 2025 General Fund transfers) means policy will remain revenue-maximising within the tribal framework — favourable to incumbents, neutral-to-positive for licensed B2B suppliers, hostile to perimeter products. **For B2Tech** the actionable path is an online gaming service provider licence targeting content/platform/payments supply to the two iGaming skins, and a watching brief on the CLC–Fanatics and tribal–operator contract cycles.
watch: DCP October 2026 iGaming release (mid-Nov 2026): first month at 20% — check whether operators trim promotional spend below the 15% cap or pass cost into hold/RTP, and whether YoY growth re-accelerates from +6%.

2027 Connecticut General Assembly session (Jan–Jun 2027): any bill to raise the 13.75% sports rate, tighten the promo deduction, expand CLC online authority (iLottery/keno), or redistribute slot-share to host towns.
Kalshi litigation and the September 2026 cease-and-desist orders to nine prediction markets — outcomes will define how far DCP can police event contracts and set precedent for other states.

Operator share trajectory: FanDuel's $27.5m YTD iGaming lead and DraftKings' sports-revenue flip; a widening iGaming gap raises the odds of a DraftKings product or promo response and tests the 15% cap.

Mohegan Sun and Foxwoods slot-win trend (DCP monthly): the ~$875m slot base funds the 25% share that anchors tribal exclusivity; sustained declines at Foxwoods (-0.75% Q1-26) would sharpen the tribes' interest in online economics.
Contract cycles: CLC–Fanatics and the tribal–DraftKings/FanDuel agreements (terms not public) — the only B2C entry points; watch for RFP signals or partner-change rumours.
Payments and KYC rule changes at DCP (credit-card funding status, instant-withdrawal standards) relevant to any B2B payments proposition [currently unverified].
